edition.name: Migne PL 3 (1844), Epistola Firmiliani ad Cyprianum, via Corpus Corporum / Latin Wikisource
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Adunatio enim et pax et concordia, non solum hominibus fidelibus et cognoscentibus veritatem, sed et Angelis ipsis coelestibus voluptatem maximam praestat, quibus dicit sermo divinus esse gaudium in uno peccatore poenitentiam agente et ad unitatis vinculum revertente. Quod utique non diceretur de Angelis conversationem in coelis habentibus, nisi ipsi quoque essent nobis adunati, qui nostra adunatione laetantur; sicut e contrario utique contristantur, quando vident diversas quorumdam mentes et scissas voluntates, quasi non tantum unum et eumdem Deum simul invocent, sed separatis et divisis ab invicem nec confabulatio jam possit esse aut sermo communis. Nisi quod nos gratiam referre Stephano in isto possumus quod per illius inhumanitatem nunc effectum sit ut fidei et sapientiae vestrae experimentum caperemus. Sed non enim si nos propter Stephanum hanc beneficii gratiam cepimus, statim Stephanus beneficio gratia digna commisit. Neque enim et Judas perfidia sua et proditione, qua scelerate circa Salvatorem operatus est, dignus videri potest quasi causam bonorum tantorum ipse praestiterit ut per illum mundus et gentium populus passione Domini liberaretur.
pass_a_gloss: For gathering and peace and harmony not only to faithful men and knowing the truth, but also to the Angels themselves heavenly gives greatest pleasure, to whom the divine word says there is joy in one sinner doing penance and returning to the bond of unity. Which certainly would not be said about Angels having conversation in heaven, unless they themselves also were gathered to us, who rejoice in our gathering; just as on the other hand they are certainly grieved, when they see diverse minds of some and split wills, as if they do not invoke one and the same God together, but separated and divided from each other and no longer conversation or common speech can be. Except that we can give thanks to Stephen in this, that through his inhumanity now it has been brought about that we experience a test of your faith and wisdom. But not if we on account of Stephen have taken this benefit of gratitude, immediately Stephen has committed a gratitude worthy of benefit. Nor indeed can Judas by his perfidy and betrayal, by which he wickedly acted around the Savior, be seen as worthy as if he himself provided the cause of so many good things that through him the world and the people of the nations were liberated by the passion of the Lord.

bible_refs.note: joy in one sinner doing penance

pass_b_english: Gathering, peace, and harmony bring the highest delight not only to faithful people who know the truth, but also to the heavenly Angels themselves; the divine word says there is joy among them over one sinner who repents and returns to the bond of unity (Luke 15:7). That would never be said of Angels who dwell in heaven unless they, too, are joined to us and rejoice in our gathering. Conversely, they are surely grieved when they see divided minds and split wills, as though those people no longer call on the one same God together, but, separated and divided from one another, can no longer share conversation or common speech. We can, however, give thanks to Stephen for this: through his inhumanity it has come about that we might test your faith and wisdom. Yet even if we have received this benefit of gratitude because of Stephen, that does not mean Stephen has performed a deed worthy of thanks. Nor can Judas be considered worthy, as if he himself supplied the cause of such great goods, so that through him the world and the nations were set free by the Lord's passion, on account of his perfidy and the betrayal by which he acted wickedly toward the Savior.

anf_compare.notes: Drafted from source only; ANF not shown to drafter.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass B correctly identifies the implied scripture (Luke 15:7) which is required for the 'sermo divinus' allusion. The distinction regarding Stephen and Judas is preserved, maintaining the author's nuance that while their actions led to good outcomes, they are not the authors of the grace/merit.
